title: Hyponatraemia
summary: Na⁺ <135 mmol/L — the urgency is set by symptoms and speed of onset, not the number alone; severe symptoms need hypertonic saline with senior support.

sources.label: European Clinical Practice Guideline on Hyponatraemia (2014)

blocks.title: Severe symptoms — treat as an emergency
blocks.body: Vomiting, seizures, reduced GCS, cardiorespiratory distress with Na⁺ <130: this needs hypertonic saline (e.g. 150 mL 2.7–3% NaCl IV over 20 min, repeated per response) — senior/critical care involvement, HDU-level monitoring, verify against local policy.

items: Confirm true hypotonic hyponatraemia: check serum osmolality; exclude hyperglycaemia (corrected Na⁺) and lab artefact
Grade symptoms: severe (seizures, GCS↓, vomiting) vs moderate (nausea, confusion, headache) vs mild/absent
Establish tempo: acute (<48 h, e.g. post-op, polydipsia, MDMA) vs chronic/unknown (assume chronic)
Assess volume status clinically: hypovolaemic, euvolaemic, or hypervolaemic
Paired tests BEFORE fluids where possible: serum osmolality, urine osmolality, urine sodium; review drugs (thiazides, SSRIs, PPIs, carbamazepine) and consider adrenal/thyroid screen

rows: Clinical volume depletion, urine Na⁺ often <30 (renal losses give >30)
Urine osmolality >100, urine Na⁺ >30, no oedema; exclude adrenal insufficiency and hypothyroidism
Fluid restriction; find and treat the cause
Oedema — heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome

blocks.title: Correction limits
blocks.body: In chronic hyponatraemia aim for a rise of no more than ~8–10 mmol/L in the first 24 h (lower if high risk of osmotic demyelination: alcohol excess, malnutrition, hypokalaemia, liver disease). Overcorrection → involve seniors early; relowering with glucose 5% ± desmopressin is a specialist decision.

blocks.title: Why speed of onset matters
blocks.body: Brain cells adapt to chronic hypotonicity by exporting osmolytes over ~48 hours. Correcting chronic hyponatraemia faster than the brain can re-accumulate them risks osmotic demyelination syndrome, whereas genuinely acute hyponatraemia carries the opposite danger — cerebral oedema — and justifies prompt, controlled hypertonic saline when symptomatic.
